deep.reconstruction:
Context (cote 154, 'système de pseudo-droites', 1983-84). Grothendieck is studying configurations of pseudolines (p.d.) in a real projective plane and the combinatorial changes they undergo under deformation. This page treats the combinatorics of moving one pseudoline D relative to a fixed configuration, denoted K_1, whose singular set (crossing points) is S(K_1). The preceding page is a drawing of oriented curves crossing near a common point, which fits this subject.

Step 1, discretising one-parameter families. Take a one-parameter family D_t of pseudolines. Cut the parameter interval into segments such that, inside each segment, the combinatorial type stays constant and the D_t stay in 'standard' (general) position with respect to K_1. The type changes only at isolated 'transition' moments, which are elementary operations (D passes through a crossing point of K_1). These are triangle flips, also called Ringel mutations or Reidemeister-III type moves.

Step 2, restriction. He restricts to pseudolines for which the double cover \tilde D is a manifold. Reading uncertain: probably \tilde D is the lift to S^2, i.e. the oriented version of D, a circle.

Step 3, polygonal structure. The set of partial transition operations of D then carries a 'polygonal structure': the graph whose vertices are combinatorial positions of p.d. and whose edges are elementary transitions has natural 2-cells (polygons). The interlinear addition seems to require compatibility with orientation.

Step 4, transporting orientation. There are two possible conventions for transporting an orientation across a transition. He chooses the 'most intuitive' one: orientations are pulled back to D by genericity, and transport of the orientation on X is opposite to the parallel transport of the orientation.

Step 5, the resulting complex X. With this convention, in the cell complex X obtained, every vertex has degree 4. The vertices are in bijection with pairs (D, a), where D is a pseudoline and a is an 'incidence edge' on \tilde D: an arc of D joining two consecutive points of D ∩ S(K_1) that contains no other point of S(K_1). This is a combinatorial dual: a 4-valent graph is what one expects for the vertices of a pseudoline arrangement, or for the 1-skeleton of the dual of a quadrangulated complex.

Step 6, the nicest case. The situation is particularly nice when the decomposition of X according to relative positions is a genuine cellular decomposition. He notes this means X is a real projective plane and D a pseudoline. The elementary operations then become interpretable in terms of the duality of these cell decompositions, via flips or 'retournements' (reading uncertain), and the page breaks off.

In modern terms, this is a description of the space of one-element extensions of a rank-3 (pseudoline) configuration by a pseudoline D:
- the cells are the combinatorial positions of D relative to K_1;
- the edges are mutations (D crossing a vertex of K_1);
- the observation is that this space, suitably oriented and cellularised, is again a projective plane carrying a dual 4-valent arrangement-like decomposition.

The next page lists marking data (marked sides, critical axes marked on edges, faces), consistent with building such a dual cell complex.
errors: No outright error can be identified given the poor legibility. The claim that a cellular decomposition 'means' X is a real projective plane is stated without argument. For the space of positions of a pseudoline relative to a simple arrangement this is plausible: the analogue of the extension space being RP^2, or S^2 in the oriented version. In general, however, cellularity of the extension space is a nontrivial issue (cf. extension space problems for oriented matroids). Rank 3 is fine, but the claim is unproven on the page.

The 1-1 correspondence 'vertices of order 4 ↔ (D, incidence edge)' is asserted without verification. It depends on the conventions (genericity, the orientation-transport convention) just chosen, which are themselves only partly legible.

ideas.what: Decompose one-parameter deformations of a pseudoline relative to a configuration into intervals of constant combinatorial type separated by elementary transitions (D passing through a crossing).
ideas.modern_name: Mutations / triangle flips of pseudoline arrangements; allowable sequences

ideas.what: The set of transitions carries a polygonal (2-cell) structure: the flip graph is filled in by polygons, with orientation conventions.
ideas.modern_name: 2-dimensional cell complex of mutations; higher Bruhat orders B(n,2), Manin–Schechtman (1989); flip complexes

ideas.what: The space X of positions of an added pseudoline D relative to K_1 is a cell complex with 4-valent vertices indexed by (D, incidence edge). When cellular, X is a real projective plane, and elementary operations become duality of cell decompositions.
ideas.modern_name: Extension space of a rank-3 oriented matroid (single-element extensions); its homotopy type (RP^2/S^2); duality via the Folkman–Lawrence topological representation
ideas.usually_credited_to: Las Vergnas (single-element extensions, 1978); Sturmfels–Ziegler, 'Extension spaces of oriented matroids' (1993); Mnëv–Ziegler

ideas.what: A choice of convention: orientation transport across transitions opposite to parallel transport, with orientations pulled back to D by genericity.
ideas.modern_name: Orientation / sign conventions on flip complexes (local coefficient systems)

missed.claim: Grothendieck treats the space of positions of one pseudoline relative to a fixed configuration as a cell complex. He asserts that in the good (cellular) case it is a real projective plane whose vertices are 4-valent, with mutations read as duality of cell decompositions. This anticipates the extension-space viewpoint for rank-3 oriented matroids. Sturmfels–Ziegler (1993) proved the rank-3 extension space has the homotopy type of a sphere; the general extension space conjecture was later disproved in higher rank (Liu, 2020). There is no indication this 1983-84 work is known or credited.
missed.quote: La situation est [particulièrement sympathique] si la [décomposition] de X ... est [cellulaire] (Ce qui signifie ... que X est un plan projectif réel, et D une p. droite)
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: It is an independent, early, and explicitly cellular/dual formulation of the rank-3 extension space. A full transcription of the surrounding pages might give an explicit combinatorial cell structure, with orientation conventions, of relevance to extension spaces and flip complexes of pseudoline arrangements.

missed.claim: The programme of interpreting elementary operations (mutations) through duality of cellular decompositions of X is announced but breaks off. The page does not show that the polygonal structure on transitions makes the flip complex simply connected, nor does it identify its 2-cells explicitly.

missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Polygon relations in flip graphs of pseudoline arrangements (squares and hexagon/octagon-type relations, cf. higher Bruhat orders and Zamolodchikov-type relations) remain an active topic. Grothendieck's orientation conventions might give a different presentation.

deep.surprise_reason: The page shows Grothendieck developing, in 1983-84, a cellular/dual picture of the space of positions of a pseudoline relative to an arrangement. In this picture, transitions form a polygonal complex, and the cellular case is a projective plane with 4-valent vertices. This is close in spirit to later work on extension spaces and flip complexes (Sturmfels–Ziegler, Manin–Schechtman) that does not reference him. However, the legibility is poor, the statements are informal, and the mathematics is natural for anyone working on pseudoline arrangements, so it is a notable but not startling unpublished detail.
